title: Sirolimus for the treatment of Graves’ orbitopathy

sections.abstract:
A role of mTOR (mammalian target of rapamycin) in the pathogenesis of Graves’ Orbitopathy (GO) has been proposed and rapamycin, better known as sirolimus, an mTOR inhibitor, was recently used in patients with GO. Here we review the available studies evaluating the role of mTOR in GO pathogenesis and the effects of sirolimus on GO.

A comprehensive search of PubMed was conducted using the following keywords: “Graves’ orbitopathy”, or “thyroid eye disease”, or “Graves’ ophthalmopathy”, or “thyroid-associated ophthalmopathy”; and: “mTOR”, or “sirolimus”, or “rapamycin”. Inclusion criteria: 1) original articles (preclinical and clinical studies); 2) English language. The articles that did not adequately explore the role of mTOR in GO pathogenesis and those in which the effects of sirolimus on GO were not investigated were excluded. At the end of the screening process, nine studies were included in this systematic review.

mTOR signaling pathway was found to be upregulated in patients with GO. In addition, studies in a mouse model of GO, in orbital fibroblasts and peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) derived from GO patients showed a significant reduction in inflammatory mediators, adipogenesis and fibrosis after treatment with sirolimus. In 2007 and 2019 two cases of patients with GO unresponsive to glucocorticoids and successfully treated with sirolimus were described. Consistently with these results, two retrospective investigations showed that treatment with sirolimus, used at low dosage for 12 weeks, was followed by a greater overall response of GO compared with methylprednisolone at 24 weeks. In addition, a good response in diplopia and ocular motility restriction after treatment with sirolimus was reported by two case series. All of these studies reported a good tolerability of sirolimus. Finally, GO response to treatment was shown to correlate with the serum levels of sirolimus at the end of treatment.

Sirolimus may represent a cheap, effective, and safe alternative treatment for GO. In addition, serum levels of sirolimus may be used to predict the response to treatment. Randomized clinical trials are needed to confirm the efficacy of sirolimus on GO and establish the best possible treatment protocol.

Keywords: Graves orbitopathy, Thyroid eye disease, Graves’ disease, Sirolimus, Rapamycin, mTOR
sections.introduction:
Graves’ orbitopathy (GO), also known as thyroid eye disease (TED), is the most common extrathyroidal manifestation of Graves’ disease (GD), being observed in ~30% of GD patients [ 1 , 2 ]. Opinion leaders in the field agree that GO is an autoimmune condition and that the main responsible autoantigen is the thyroid stimulating hormone receptor (TSH-R). Once activated by autoantibodies or autoreactive T-cells, TSH-R interacts with the insulin-like growth factor 1-receptor (IGF-1 R) [ 3 ]. The crosstalk between TSH-R and IGF-1 R, together with a series of mechanisms involving mononuclear cells, cytokines, and oxidative stress, leads to orbital fibroblast proliferation, adipogenesis and release of great amounts of glycosaminoglycans, especially hyaluronic acid [ 3 ]. These events ultimately lead to inflammation and fibrosis and result in the modifications of the orbital content and in the clinical manifestations of GO [ 3 ]. Quality of life of affected patients is strongly impaired by the visual disability and aesthetic disfigurement [ 4 ].

According to the guidelines of the European Group On Graves’ Orbitopathy (EUGOGO), the first-line treatment of moderate-to-severe, active GO is high dose intravenous glucocorticoids (ivGCs) associated with mycophenolate given orally [ 4 ]. The recent acquisitions on GO pathogenesis have led to the introduction of new target therapies. The most relevant are teprotumumab, tocilizumab, rituximab and batoclimab. Among these, teprotumumab, an anti-IGF-1 R monoclonal antibody, was shown to be the most effective. To date, two placebo-controlled, randomized clinical trials (RCTs) have been conducted in patients with moderate-to-severe and active GO [ 5 , 6 ]. A pooled analysis combining data on the two RCTs showed, at 24 weeks, a mean reduction in proptosis of 3.14 mm in patients treated with teprotumumab vs 0.37 mm in those given placebo [ 7 ]. Furthermore, teprotumumab was associated with a higher prevalence of proptosis responders (reduction ≥2 mm) (77% vs 15%), disease inactivation [clinical activity score (CAS) ≤1] (63% vs 21%) and diplopia responders (improvement by at least 1 grade in Gorman score) (70% vs 31%) [ 7 ]. Teprotumumab was found to be highly effective in improving proptosis also in patients with inactive (CAS ≤1) GO of long duration (2–10 years) [ 8 ]. Despite its efficacy, long-term follow-up of patients treated with teprotumumab revealed a relatively high relapse rate (⁓30%) [ 9 , 10 ]. Furthermore, its association with hyperglycemia and, particularly, with hearing impairments [ 7 ], raises concerns about a diffuse use of teprotumumab in GO. Notably, in a prospective, longitudinal study, otological symptoms were reported in 22/27 patients (81.5%), and among the 11 patients who developed hearing loss/decreased word recognition, complete resolution was observed in only 5 cases (45.5%) [ 11 ].

Unlike teprotumumab, tocilizumab and rituximab have shown conflicting results. Tocilizumab is an anti-IL-6 receptor monoclonal antibody. In a RCT, tocilizumab was found to be effective in improving disease activity in patients with moderate-to-severe, active GO resistant to ivGCs [ 12 ]. However, no significant effect on proptosis and diplopia was observed [ 12 ]. Furthermore, its efficacy remains uncertain due to the lack of additional clinical studies. Similarly, the efficacy of rituximab, a monoclonal antibody against CD20, is yet to be fully established. One RCT reported significant improvements in CAS and higher rates of disease inactivation compared with ivGCs [ 13 ]. However, a second RCT failed to demonstrate a higher efficacy of rituximab compared with placebo [ 14 ]. Furthermore, no effect on proptosis and diplopia was found [ 13 , 14 ]. Finally, batoclimab, an anti-neonatal fragment crystallizable receptor (FcRn) monoclonal antibody, is another emerging, alternative treatment for GO. FcRn rescues IgG, including TRAb, from lysosomal degradation, thereby prolonging their circulating half-time [ 15 ]. Batoclimab blocks FcRn-mediated recycling of IgG, which results in reduction in IgG levels [ 16 ]. In a phase 2b RCT, batoclimab was found to be associated with a higher proptosis response rate (reduction ≥2 mm) compared to placebo at several intermediate evaluations during treatment. However, no significant difference between batoclimab and placebo was observed at 12 weeks (primary outcome), namely at the end of treatment. In addition, no significant effect on diplopia was observed, and disease inactivation (CAS ≤1) was more frequent in patients treated with batoclimab only at 5 and 11 weeks [ 17 ].

In view of these considerations, the development of novel treatments for GO remains highly warranted. Recently, mTOR (mammalian target of rapamycin) was shown to be involved in the pathogenesis of GO, leading to the use of rapamycin, better known as sirolimus, an mTOR inhibitor, in patients with GO. We therefore conducted a systematic review aimed at analyzing the available evidence on the role of mTOR and on the efficacy of sirolimus in GO and discusses the possible future implications in this field.
sections.methods:
A systematic review was conducted up to 07 May 2025, according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) statement guidelines [ 18 ]. A comprehensive search of PubMed was conducted using the following string: (“Graves’ orbitopathy” OR “Graves’ disease” OR “thyroid eye disease” OR “Graves’ ophthalmopathy” OR “thyroid-associated ophthalmopathy”) AND (“mTOR” OR “sirolimus” OR “rapamycin”). The following inclusion criteria were applied: 1) original articles, including both preclinical and clinical studies; 2) studies published in English. Studies were excluded if they did not adequately address the role of mTOR or the effects of sirolimus on GO or did not meet the inclusion criteria. The title, abstract, and full text of the results were screened by two independent investigators. After screening the studies using the inclusion and exclusion criteria, nine studies were included in this review. The detailed selection strategy of the studies is shown in Fig. 1 .

PRISMA flow diagram representing the search strategy

Before presenting the results of the selected studies, we provide a general overview of the mTOR signaling pathway and characteristics of sirolimus to facilitate a better understanding of the topic.
sections.discussion:
The data reviewed so far suggest that sirolimus holds promise as a novel therapeutic option for patients with GO, especially in cases characterized by inflammatory and fibrotic features. Based on studies in vitro and in animal models, sirolimus may act in GO through multiple mechanisms involving mTORC1 inhibition: suppression of cytotoxic CD4 + T cell activity, downregulation of proinflammatory cytokines like IL-16, and reduction of fibroblast-mediated tissue remodeling via inhibition of the IGF-1 R–Src–mTOR axis. These combined effects could translate into both immunomodulatory and antifibrotic therapeutic benefits in GO. Clinical studies, although mostly retrospective and involving small sample sizes, have reported improvements in disease activity, diplopia, and quality of life after treatment with sirolimus, which was associated with a favorable safety profile. Overall, observations from preclinical experiments are consistent with, and provide explanations to results from clinical studies. In particular, improvement in CAS may be the result of the inhibitory action of sirolimus on IL-16 release and, consequently, on the recruitment of lymphocytes in the orbital tissues. Additionally, sirolimus directly decreases the activity of CD4+ T-cells, which further contributes to explaining the improvement of GO activity observed in some clinical studies. On the other hand, treatment with sirolimus was associated with remarkable effects on disease severity, especially on EOM and diplopia, in patients with moderate-to-severe or severe GO. These results find a pathophysiological explanation in the inhibitory effect of sirolimus on orbital adipogenesis and fibrosis observed in two in vitro studies [ 62 , 64 ].

Current clinical evidence indicates that sirolimus, used as second-line treatment, is associated with a higher efficacy on GO compared with methylprednisolone, even in settings where ivGCs have been administered as first-line treatment. Therefore, it may be postulated that sirolimus could achieve greater therapeutic benefit if used as an initial treatment strategy in patients with newly diagnosed GO.

The therapeutic paradigm of GO is undergoing profound changes due to the introduction of novel pharmacological agents, most notably teprotumumab [ 5 – 7 ]. As previously reported, clinical trials showed this monoclonal antibody to be remarkably effective on patients with GO, and led to its approval in some Countries. Nevertheless, GO relapse following treatment discontinuation remains a significant clinical concern, occurring in approximately 30% of cases [ 9 , 10 ]. In view of these considerations, sirolimus may represent a promising therapeutic alternative for patients experiencing disease recurrence after a first course of teprotumumab. Furthermore, in cases in which teprotumumab cannot be administered (owing to contraindications or financial constraints), sirolimus could warrant consideration as a potential first-line alternative to methylprednisolone.

The relatively low cost of sirolimus represents another important, practical advantage over other treatments. A 12-week course of sirolimus, used at the same dosage as in the above-mentioned retrospective studies, requires a total of 87 tablets, which approximately results in a cost of 367.04 US dollars ( http://www.pharmacychecker.com ) or 290.43 Euros ( https://www.bbfarma.com/index-en.html ). The cost of ivGCs is slightly lower ($ 172/€ 70) [ 63 ], but it does not include administration costs. On the contrary, the cost of all the other medical treatments currently available for GO largely exceed that of sirolimus: about $14,519/€ 4,266 for a complete course of tocilizumab, $ 19,636/€ 4,308 for rituximab, and $357,997 for a complete course of teprotumumab in a 75 kg patient [ 71 ].

Beyond the economic consideration, oral administration represents another advantage of sirolimus over other treatments for GO. Indeed, unlike intravenous regimens, oral administration improves patient compliance and does not require nursing staff or dedicated facilities. However, this route is associated with greater variability in serum drug levels, which, in the case of sirolimus, is mainly due to differences in intestinal CYP3A4 expression [ 51 ]. Nonetheless, this limitation may be overcome by monitoring serum drug concentrations. A direct correlation between sirolimus trough levels and GO response has been already reported in a retrospective study [ 69 ]. Furthermore, in clinical settings for which sirolimus is approved, its trough concentrations, measured in the morning prior to drug administration, are routinely used to adjust dosing in order to maintain serum levels within a defined target range. On the contrary, current evidence is insufficient to define the optimal target range and timing of sirolimus levels monitoring in GO. Further clinical studies, ideally prospective and randomized, are warranted to address these questions and to assess therapeutic drug monitoring should be adopted in this setting.

Despite these advantages, the available studies are insufficient to support the routine use of sirolimus in clinical practice due to the following limitations. First of all, the quality of evidence provided by these studies is relatively low because of their nature: most of them are case reports or case series, whereas only three retrospective studies have been conducted so far. In addition, all of the retrospective studies included a small sample size, and one of them compared the use of sirolimus as second-line treatment with ivGCs given as first-line treatment [ 68 ]. Another relevant limitation is the wide variation in sirolimus dosage and treatment durations across studies. This inconsistency makes it challenging to directly compare their findings. In this context, prospective RCTs are warranted to provide stronger evidence on the efficacy and safety of sirolimus in GO patients. In addition, RCTs could define more accurately the characteristics of GO patients who would benefit most from treatment with sirolimus. RCTs would also clarify the optimal dosage, treatment duration, and positioning of sirolimus in the therapeutic algorithm of GO. Future studies should also explore whether prolonged treatment or combination with other therapies might enhance the long-term benefits of mTOR inhibition in this setting. Results from a retrospective study suggested that extended treatment with sirolimus may be associated with better long-term outcomes in GO [ 68 ]. However, this hypothesis requires confirmation through RCTs specifically design to compare different treatment durations. Such a trial would also provide valuable insights into the safety profile associated with prolonged therapy. Indeed, extended treatment with sirolimus might negatively impact tolerability, as the risk of some adverse events, especially IGT and type 2 diabetes, were shown to increase with long-term use. However, whether this risk persists at relatively low doses of sirolimus remains to be established.
sections.conclusion: Sirolimus represents a promising, cost-effective candidate for the treatment of GO, with the potential to expand the available therapeutic options, particularly for patients with GO resistant to standard treatments. However, randomized clinical trials are needed to confirm the efficacy of sirolimus on GO and to find the most effective and safe therapeutic regimen.
